entries.title: Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to collusion
entries.summary: The prominent activist pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign entities. He faces a lengthy prison sentence.
entries.content:
Hong Kong

Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty to collusion

September 2, 2026

The prominent activist pleaded guilty to colluding with foreign entities. He faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Pro-democracy Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong on Wednesday pleaded guilty to a charge of colluding with foreign entities.

Wong, who is already serving a nearly five-year prison sentence for subversion, was due to be released next year and could face up to life in prison.

What was Wong accused of?

Wong was accused of conspiring with fellow activist Nathan Law and others to ask foreign countries, or institutions, organizations, or individuals to impose sanctions or engage in other hostile actions against Hong Kong or China between July and November, 2020.

Wong sat in the courtroom dock as the charges were read out, before confirming his guilty plea, AFP journalists reported from inside the court.

He smiled and nodded after someone in the public gallery shouted "hang in there!"

Among those attending proceedings were several Western diplomats.

Who is Joshua Wong?

Wong first became widely known in Hong Kong as a teenager in 2012 when he led protests against national education being introduced in the city's school.

In 2014, he rose to fame as one of the student leaders in the city's Occupy Movement, during which demonstrators occupied streets for 79 days while calling for direct elections for Hong Kong's leader.

However, Wong's efforts to garner overseas support for protests angered Beijing, which labelled him an advocate of Hong Kong independence who had "begged for interference" from foreign forces.

The political party he co-founded, Demosisto, was disbanded after the security law was enacted on June 30, 2020.

The 29-year-old was among dozens of activists arrested in 2021 for taking part in an unofficial poll to select candidates for a 2020 legislative council election.

His protest efforts have effectively been outlawed by Beijing's sweeping national security law, introduced in Hong Kong in 2020, following major protests.

Critics say Wong’s case illustrates the lengths to which authorities are willing to go to silence prominent dissidents.

More to follow…

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up
entries.summary: Explosions have been reported around the Strait of Hormuz, including at an airport in southern Iran. US President Donald Trump said the strikes were a response to Iranian attempts to mine the strait. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US, Tehran trade fire in new flare-up

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Explosions have been reported around the Strait of Hormuz, including at an airport in southern Iran. US President Donald Trump said the strikes were a response to Iranian attempts to mine the strait. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Below is a roundup of the top headlines on the Iran war and other developments in the Middle East region on Tuesday, September 1, 2026.

  • US military says it has launched strikes on Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)
  • US President Trump described the strikes as 'large and powerful'
  • Iran said the US would 'regret' the latest attacks
  • Jordanian military says it intercepted Iranian missiles in Jordanian airspace
  • Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq's Kurdistan region also targeted by Iranian attacks

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

WATCH: Fighting Iran war, can US military sustain a long conflict?

Six months into the Iran war, US military leaders are warning of stretched forces and depleted weapons stockpiles. Does the US have the resources to keep fighting?

Skip next section Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region

Iran's Revolutionary Guards say US bases targeted in Iraq's Kurdistan region

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had launched strikes on US bases with drones and missiles in Erbil, Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, according to state media.

State -run IRNA reported that the IRGC said they had "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" and had destroyed a maintenance facility, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat."

The claims cannot be independently verified. The US military has not yet commented on the matter.

Skip next section Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones

Air alert sirens sound in Bahrain, Kuwait intercepts Iranian drones

Sirens warning of potential aerial threats sounded in Bahrain early on Wednesday amid the latest escalation between the US and Iran. 

Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said in a post on X: "A danger is present. The Ministry of Interior calls upon citizens and residents to adhere to calm, head to the nearest safe place, and follow the news through official channels, to safeguard public safety.

Bahrain is home to a major US naval base where the 5th Fleet is headquartered and has previously been targeted by Tehran.

Kuwait, another US ally in the Mideast region, also said it repelled attacks by "hostile" Iranian drones.

Skip next section US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran

US military says it completed strikes on targets in Iran

US Central Command (CENTCOM) said that its latest wave of strikes against Iranian military targets has been completed.

"U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," CENTCOM said in a statement.

It went on to say that the strikes came after "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members."

CENTCOM said there were currently 50,000 US military personnel operating in the Middle East.

Skip next section Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted

Jordan's military says Iranian missiles intercepted

The Jordanian Armed Forces said that 10 ballistic missiles launched from Iran had been intercepted, while another three landed in remote areas.

"Jordan's air defence systems engaged 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them, while three missiles fell in remote areas away from populated centres," a Jordanian military statement stated. Jordan added that no casualties had been reported.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump said that the latest strikes on Iran had been in response to Iranian missile launches at US targets on Monday and attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.

"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.

"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."

He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."

Skip next section US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back

US launches strikes on Iran, Tehran fires back

The United States has launched fresh strikes on targets in Iran as hostilities once again flare up. 

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

"The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait," US President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social platform.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump warned.

Earlier, Trump told US broadcaster Fox News that US forces had struck Iranian radars.

“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump told Fox. “We waited until it was almost built and then we hit it."

An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, located around 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The US military announced it has launched new strikes on targets in Iran. Iran has vowed retaliation. 

The Iran war has been fought intermittently for the past 6 months and with the latest round of hostilities, there doesn't appear to be an end in sight to the conflict that is having major global economic repercussions.

Stay with us for updates and analysis on unfolding events in both Iran and the wider Middle East region.

entries.title: Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response
entries.summary: Any escalation in the Baltic region will lead to a significant response, Moscow said.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Russia threatens 'devastating' Baltic response

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 2, 2026

Any escalation in the Baltic region will lead to a significant response, Moscow said.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading!

Follow this blog for the latest news on Russia's war in Ukraine on September 1, 2026.

  • Russian strikes Kyiv, Odesa on first day of school year, killing at least 12
  • EU ministers focus on Ukraine air defenses, military support at Ireland talks
  • Drones trigger brief NATO response at Estonia's border with Russia

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section 'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

'Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,' Zelenskyy warns

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines flying across Russia, saying that Ukraine's drone operations would make the airspace unsafe.

"Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said in a statement on Tuesday evening. He said that Ukraine was not threatening civilian aviation or individual aircraft.

"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said.

Just last week, Zelenskyy threatened the deployment of up to 1,000 long-range drones per day.

Russian President Vladimir Putin branded Zelenskyy's comments "a declaration of state terrorism."

"They are asking us to resume negotiations... but you don't negotiate with terrorists," Putin said in a televised news conference.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022 and has repeatedly managed to strike targets deep inside Russia with drones as part of its defense efforts.

Skip next section Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry

Vessels hit near Odesa: Russia Defense Ministry

Russia's military struck two cargo ships carrying military goods, the country's Defense Ministry said.

The vessels were hit in the port of Pivdennyi, ​near ​the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, ​and ‌in the Black ​Sea.

Skip next section Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure

Russia, Ukraine hit each other's energy infrastructure

A Russian strike caused damage to a thermal power plant in the region of Odesa, southern Ukraine, state energy company Naftogaz said.

Elsewhere, Ukraine's military intelligence said that a strike by the Ukrainian army hit Russia's Novatek oil complex in the region of Leningrad.

Kyiv and Moscow have been exchanging blows in the past 24 hours, with energy infrastructure being targeted as part of the mutual strikes.

Skip next section Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions

Russia threatens 'devastating' response amid Baltic tensions

Russia says it will "deliver a devastating response" to any hostile action against it in the Baltic region.

"In the event of a further escalation of the military-political situation in the Baltic region, it must be emphasized once again: Russia's response to the instigators of reckless anti-Russian ventures will be decisive. And they need to know this - it will be devastating for them," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at her weekly briefing.

It's not exactly clear what she was referring to, but earlier in the day a fire broke out at Russia's Baltic port of Ust-Luga following a drone attack according to the regional governor.

Separately, NATO scrambled military aircraft due to a possible air threat in Latvia's airspace near the town of Ludza, close to the Russian border.

Skip next section Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium

Russia sees no peace gains from Black Sea attack moratorium

Russia does not believe a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, a key grain shipping route, would bring a peaceful resolution to the war closer, Interfax quoted Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko as saying Tuesday.

Both sides have stepped up attacks in the Black Sea in recent months, driving global grain prices higher.

In mid-August, Ukraine reportedly conveyed an offer to Russia through a third party proposing that both sides halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea.

Monday, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his country had prepared a plan to ensure the safe passage of grain through the Black Sea and was working on an agreement similar to the 2022 grain deal that would facilitate safe exports.

Skip next section EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.

"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.

"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.

Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.

"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.

Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.

Skip next section Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. 

Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.

The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.

Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."

"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."

Skip next section Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.

The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.

At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:

  • Seven people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; three others were wounded, including a child.
  • One Indian citizen was reported among those killed
  • One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district after a building was hit and caught fire.
  • Three people were killed and 12 were injured elsewhere in the Kyiv region.

In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."

Skip next section Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.

The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.

He did not immediately provide additional details.

Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."

At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.

Skip next section EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.

Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.

There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.

The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.

The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.

The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.

Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.

EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.

Skip next section NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO military aircraft were scrambled overnight after drones flew close to Estonia's border and briefly entered Estonian airspace, the country's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

The aircraft were launched from Amari Air Base, Tsahkna wrote in a post on social media.

"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned. The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory," he added.

It was not immediately clear who launched the drones.

The incident highlights ongoing security concerns along NATO's eastern flank and is seen as a consequence of Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.

Skip next section Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russia targeted Ukraine's capital for a sixth day in a row, including a ballistic missile strike on a railway depot in Kyiv that killed seven people.

"The ballistic strike took the lives of 7 people, 6 of whom were our employees. 1 colleague is in hospital with injuries," Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chief executive of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state-owned railway network said, adding that "there is extensive destruction."

Emergency services said eight people were killed and five wounded in Kyiv, including three children, as fires broke out across several parts of the capital during the overnight attacks.

Elsewhere in the Kyiv region, one person was killed and nine others, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones struck an apartment building and a business facility in Boryspil.

The attacks marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and nearby areas.

Across the border in Russia's Belgorod region, one person was killed in a Ukrainian attack, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

European defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today and are expected to hear from Ukraine's new acting defense minister, Yevgeniy Khmara.

He is likely to point to the latest wave of Russian attacks, now entering a sixth straight day, as Moscow continues its campaign against Kyiv and surrounding areas.

Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.

The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.

Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.

We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

entries.title: Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
entries.summary: Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August. The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible."
entries.content:
Germany

Germany blames Russia for attempted airport drone attack

September 2, 2026

Investigators believe an explosives-laden drone was deliberately targeting a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle airport in early August. The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible."

The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. 

"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin .

Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?

"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.

He said the attack fit the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.

Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.

Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport. 

German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."

"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday.

"We do not view Leipzig as an isolated incident, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions," he continued. "We assume that Germany will be the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia."

How will Germany respond?

Dobrindt insisted that Germany is "not at war" but that it is "a daily target of hybrid warfare."

Therefore, he said, Germany would respond to the hybrid attack in Leipzig in a "proportionate and measured, yet resolute manner."

Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany's response would be coordinated closely with European Union and NATO partners.

"We are tightening entry controls for Russian nationals" and Berlin would propose the listing of more Russian individuals for European Union sanctions, Wadephul said, as the Russian ambassador to Berlin was summoned.

In addition to a strengthening of internal security, he also announced additional measures including the closure of the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn from September 18 and the rescinding of a contract enabling the operation of the "Russian House," a Russian cultural center in Berlin.

"Our message to the Russian leadership is clear," Germany's top diplomat said. "We are sticking to our security course. The attack on Leipzig shows that this is necessary. We will not allow our social cohesion to be divided by Russian attacks. We remain ready to react along with our partners when the protection of our population demands it."

Finally, he said that Germany would continue to support Ukraine in its "defensive battle against Russian aggression."

How have NATO and the EU responded?

"NATO stands ​in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid ​attack in Leipzig on 14 August," ⁠said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, adding that the alliance would continue strengthening its ability to deter and defend ‌its ⁠allies ⁠against threats.

"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he added.

"The German government has taken strong measures and the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

"We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression," she continued. "We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security. Russia is seeking to sow distrust and fear among our societies. But it will fail. And we will stand by Ukraine for as long as it takes."

The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,

Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.

How have Russia and Ukraine responded?

Russia's President Vladimir Putin rejected Berlin’s allegations, claiming Germany's leadership was attempting use the incident to deflect from their own failings and dissatisfaction among voters with "the need to counter an aggressive Russia."

Putin also claimed Russia was being set up.

"But where is the proof? Well, the proof has been planted," Putin told reporters in the early hours of Wednesday in Kyrgyzstan.

Ukraine meanwhile, welcomed Berlin's measures against Russia following the failed drone attack at Leipzig airport.

Ukrainian Ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev praised Berlin's response late on Tuesday.

"I welcome Germany's resolute response to the Russian attack in Leipzig," Makeiev wrote on social media platform X.

Kyiv has been in close contact with Berlin to secure critical infrastructure against drones, a coordinated approach against Russia's "shadow fleet" and further sanctions against Moscow, he said.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again
entries.summary: Explosions were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as at an airport in southern Iran. US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran: US launches fresh strikes as hostilities flare again

September 1, 2026

Explosions were reported in and around the Strait of Hormuz, as well as at an airport in southern Iran. US President Trump described the strikes as "large and powerful." Iran said the US will "regret" its latest attacks.

Hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz flared up again on Tuesday evening as the United States launched fresh strikes on Iranian targets in and around the strategic waterway.

"Explosions were heard again in Bandar Abbas city and Qeshm island," Iranian state television reported, adding that blasts were also heard on Lavan island, home to one of Iran's Gulf oil export terminals.

Oil prices rose in the wake of the latest attacks with US crude up by as much as 5%.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed the strikes, saying they were in response to "recent attempted attacks by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region."

US President Donald Trump said the strikes, which he described as "large and powerful," were retaliation for "failed" Iranian attempts to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and the firing of "eight missiles" towards a US military base in Jordan, all of which he claimed were shot down.

"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," Trump wrote in his latest social media threat. "But it will not be the biggest attack of them all. That is waiting in the wings."

Iran: IRGC vows to respond to US strikes

An IRGC spokesman, quoted by the Fars state news agency, said the US would "regret" its latest attacks, which state television said included a strike on Jiroft airport in southeastern Iran, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) inland from the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's joint military command said its armed forces would deliver what they described as "crushing and devastating blows" against the US, while state media said the army had launched operations against unspecified US targets in the region.

The Tasnim news agency said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun. The US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones."

G20: US threatens further sanctions on Iran

Meanwhile, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that his department was planning to impose fresh sanctions on Iran.

"We are probably going to announce a bank sanction this week, and we will announce one the week after," Bessent said on the sidelines of the G20 meeting of finance ministers in North Carolina.

"We are speaking to our allies here, who have all come forward, and we have had a great show of support."

He also said the US was considering airplane leasing companies and other companies which continue to do business with the IRGC.

"We have zero tolerance," he said. "We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime."

Iran's Pezeshkian meets Putin

The latest flare-up comes just hours after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said earlier on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

Pezeshkian, speaking after the US and Iran had already resumed exchanges of fire for the first time in over a month, accused Washington of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.

Pezeshkian was speaking on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he also met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday.

Putin reportedly told Pezeshkian that Russia stood in solidarity with Iran, and that the two countries would maintain their economic relationships despite the current turbulence.

Pezeshkian thanked Putin and criticized the US for having "no right" to impose sanctions on other countries.

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

entries.title: Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
entries.summary: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest outbreaks in history.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has surpassed 6,000 confirmed cases, with nearly 3,000 deaths. As the virus spreads, authorities are racing to contain one of the deadliest outbreaks in history.

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.

"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.

"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.

Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.

"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.

The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.

"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."

Vaccination campaign gathers momentum

As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.

The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.

Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.

"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.

Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.

"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.

"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.

Communities seek protection

Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.

"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.

Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji

Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.

"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.

Violence hampers response

The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.

Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.

"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.

Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.

Economic toll grows

Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.

Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.

Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.

"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.

To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.

"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.

Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.

"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"

Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.

"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.

Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.

Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

entries.title: Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House
entries.summary: Germany has announced the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is a hub for propaganda and espionage.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany terminates lease for Berlin's Russian House

September 1, 2026

Germany has announced the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the heart of Berlin. Critics have long said it is a hub for propaganda and espionage.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has announced that the contract under which the Russian House is operated will be rescinded. This is one of several measures in retaliation for Russian involvement in the attempted airport drone attack at the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. 

The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state, its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore.

French authorities have previously linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services.

"In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations, the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin at the beginning of August. 

Back then, in response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that the fate of the Russian House is linked to that of the Goethe Institut in Moscow, and that any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other. 

German tax money for Russian propaganda?

The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation.

Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany.

Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian." 

Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website.

The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda.

Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, films were shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis.

Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow

The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes.

Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term.

Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine.

It is an open secret that the German government has been shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow.

The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia.

A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts.

So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year.

Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible

In recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations."

This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties.

Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible.

This article was originally written in German and first published in August 2025. It was updated and republished in September 2026 to reflect news developments.

entries.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis
entries.summary: Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.
entries.content:
Iran

War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis

September 1, 2026

Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.

Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country's gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations are closing before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say lines at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters (ca. 4 million gallons) a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.

Hours in line for a few liters

A resident of Karaj, a city west of the capital, Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around 5 liters (about 1.3 gallons).

"I'm in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far," he said. "Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues."

He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds, but again found a long line.

He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that could not be independently verified.

For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

"Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road," one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.

Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.

For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.

Is Iran adulteratingits gasoline?

The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.

Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.

The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran's refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.

Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements. But the timing has fueled public suspicion.

Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.

Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In the city of Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had been mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems.

Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.

Distrust over fuel quality grows

For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believed poor-quality gasoline had caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.

He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.

Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.

The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.

Tehran has argued that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.

But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.

Is a price increase in the works?

Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.

The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.

"Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers," Mansour told DW.

But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour pointed to the financial condition of Iran's oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.

When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argued, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.

Raising gasoline prices could, therefore, serve both as a demand management measure and a source of additional revenue.

A politically dangerous choice

The government has few easy options.

While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.

Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.

Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.

Today, the economic environment is considerably more fragile.

The war has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel lines are just another source of frustration.

For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.

But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
entries.summary: Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.

The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.

How much is climate change to blame?

The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact." 

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream."

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.

"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze.

Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."

"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze.

"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.

But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze.

"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."

For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.

Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.

However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal."

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.

A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning
entries.summary: The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton peace agreement ended the war, not the divisions that produced it.
entries.content:
Bosnia and Herzegovina

Mladic's death, Bosnia and Serbia's unfinished reckoning

September 1, 2026

The death of Ratko Mladic did not close a dark chapter of European history; it reopened old wounds. The ideology that created him lives on. The Dayton peace agreement ended the war, not the divisions that produced it.

The death of Ratko Mladic should have closed one of the darkest chapters in European history.

Instead, it has reopened old wounds, proving that both the Dayton Accords that ended the 1992-95 Bosnian war and the three decades of international engagement that followed never came close to addressing the causes that led to the conflict.

When Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb army, died on August 27, 2026 in a prison hospital in The Hague, his conviction for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — including the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and the siege of Sarajevo — had been final for nearly a decade.

What was never settled, however — and what, it seems, was never even seriously attempted — is the question of how a society lives with a man who remains a convicted criminal in the eyes of an international court but is viewed by some as a hero and symbol of the Serbian people.

For this reason, the reactions that followed Mladic's death came as no surprise.

Mladic openly mourned in Republika Srpska

In Serbia and the Serb-dominated Republika Srpska, one of the two semi-autonomous entities created within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, Mladic's death was mourned as the loss of a national hero, not the end of an era of crimes — a narrative that stands in direct contradiction to the facts established by international courts.

Senior officials in Republika Srpska, which covers around 49% of the territory of the former Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, called on citizens to gather in squares and light candles "for the salvation of the general's soul."

Milorad Dodik, still the most powerful political figure in Republika Srpska despite stepping down as its president last year after a six-year ban on holding public office imposed by Bosnia's constitutional court, called Mladic's death a "murder," suggesting it was "an organized approach that was meant to lead to a fatal outcome."

In Banja Luka, the de facto capital of Republika Srpska, Mayor Drasko Stanivukovic expressed his condolences to Mladic's family and confirmed that Mladic is not perceived as a man convicted of genocide but as a symbol of "a time and a struggle."

Institutional support in Belgrade

In the Serbian capital, Belgrade, this stance received institutional backing.

Serbia's justice minister announced a funeral with the highest state and military honors.

President Aleksandar Vucic accused the tribunal in The Hague of "uncivilized behavior" for not allowing Mladic to spend his final days outside his prison cell.

Former Interior Minister Aleksandar Vulin spoke of Mladic in the same breath as other Serbian national heroes, invoking a narrative linking World War I to the 1990s, saying, "From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed tied up."

A very different response elsewhere in Bosnia

In the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the other main entity in Bosnia, where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, news of Mladic's death was met with unanimous condemnation of the deceased, given that Mladic was finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, a town in eastern Bosnia where around 8,000 men and boys were killed in July 1995.

Bosnia's foreign minister, Elmedin Konakovic, framed the official Serbian response as Serbia's conscious choice. "No one is forcing Serbia to treat Mladic as a hero, nor to attribute his crimes to it. Serbia is choosing this itself," he said.

Representatives of victims and survivors pointed out that any public glorification is a direct insult to the families of those killed.

The European Commission, responding to questions about the announced state funeral, said that "glorifying convicted war criminals is contrary to the most basic European values" and that such practices have no place in either member states or candidate countries.

The European Movement in Serbia warned that a state funeral would amount to "institutional glorification" and a "serious moral, legal and political attack on Serbia." It urged the Serbian government to abandon the plan.

How can this happen?

But how is it possible that a man who has been finally convicted of genocide in Srebrenica is still honored as a military commander?

The answer is not simply that he is viewed by some as a national hero. It is structural, and it begins with the Dayton peace agreement itself.

The 1995 Dayton Accords ended the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina by turning existing front lines and territorial control into the constitutional architecture of a new state.

One of the fundamental elements of the agreement was Republika Srpska, which is recognized by all signatories and embedded in the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

That division was not an administrative technicality; it reflected the political reality on the ground at the time negotiations were held, including territories under the control of forces commanded by Mladic.

The compromise was necessary to stop the bloodshed. The problem is that since 1995, it has never been accompanied by a mechanism for dealing with the past that would match the political compromise.

Dayton created a complex constitutional architecture — a state divided into two entities and the Brcko District with a total 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — for a country of just 3 million people.

It is a system built to prevent war, not a system built to produce common citizenship, and was described by the Council of Europe's Venice Commission as long ago as 2005 as "neither rational nor efficient."

In such a system, where ethnic identity is built into the very logic of power, denial or relativization of crimes is not a marginal phenomenon, it is a political resource.

In other words, each side sees itself as a victim, which makes joint recognition of committed evil as a precondition for reconciliation impossible.

Price of missed responsibility

Bosnia-Herzegovina has state-level legislation that criminalizes the public denial, gross minimization or justification of genocide and the glorification of persons convicted of such acts.

In reality, however, enforcement of this legislation remains uneven.

Serbia has no such law, and its public authorities, instead of distancing themselves from Mladic's legacy, openly embrace it.

This is not just a symbolic difference, it is the difference between treating the wartime legacy as something shameful to be overcome or as a resource to be politically exploited.

Dayton Accords helped maintain status quo

The international community, which stopped the war in 1995 through force and diplomacy, has subsequently retreated into the role of administrator of the status quo.

The Office of the High Representative, the international envoy empowered to impose laws and remove obstructive politicians under the Dayton Accords, did indeed impose laws and remove obstructive politicians for decades. But in doing so it only stabilized the system without dismantling its causes.

The result is twofold: a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 30 years since the end of the war, and the fact that an ideology that gave rise to that war is still very much alive.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan
